source.title: Representational Difference Explanations
source.authors: Neehar Kondapaneni; Oisin Mac Aodha; P. Perona

record.tranche_reason: Tests how measurements of representational differences vary with distance-normalization choices, using BSR rather than the claim’s original similarity measures. It does not test convergence with scale.
record.gate_note: The study compares representations to explain their differences, but does not measure whether alignment rises with model size or capability. The extracted rows are limited to reported results showing sensitivity of the difference assessment to the distance metric. The BSR comparisons of explanation-method performance and qualitative explanation examples are not themselves measures of convergence.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes RDX, an explanation method for finding differences between two representations, and evaluates it against dictionary-learning baselines. It never measures whether independently trained models' representations converge, with scale or otherwise. The PRH and Convergent Learning papers appear only as citations in related work. The distance-variant results (Table A7, Fig. A13/A14, Sec. B.6) are ablations of the authors' own method and its BSR evaluation metric. They do not measure how sensitive representational-similarity estimates are, so they do not bear on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is not right. The authors conclude that RDX, a training-free method, isolates differences between two representations. They report that it recovers known differences (modified MNIST, CUB PCBM) where dictionary-learning XAI baselines fail, and that it surfaces interpretable unknown differences between DINO and DINOv2 and between CLIP and CLIP-iNat. RDX has the best BSR and Redundancy scores. Sensitivity to distance normalization is only an appendix ablation, not a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces RDX, which contrasts normalized pairwise distances and samples difference explanations; it does not reproduce either original study’s method. Its metric-sensitivity analysis uses BSR and alternative distance normalizations.
record.method_sensitivity: Distance normalization and similarity metric affect the reported BSR results. The paper reports that locally scaled distances yield poor, direction-dependent BSR results; neighborhood and max-normalized distances behave differently.

fits_no_version.finding: Locally scaled Euclidean distances make one comparison direction score near-perfect and the other poor. The authors conclude that these distances are not comparable across two representations (Sec. B.6, Fig. A14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-representation normalizations of pairwise distances (e.g. local scaling) can make cross-model distance comparisons asymmetric and unreliable.

record.problems: The metric-sensitivity results are limited to the tested distance variants and comparisons. The paper states that BSR is a proxy and should be accompanied by qualitative results; locally scaled distances are reported as unsuitable for comparing across representations.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table A3 and Fig. A13/A14 results comparing explanation-method performance or difference-function choices, except for the explicit BSRLS failure in r9; these results primarily assess RDX and its baselines rather than convergence itself. Omitted the in-distribution concept-consistency analysis in Sec. A.5 because it evaluates stability of extracted clusters, not alignment of representations.

untested.parts: All of it; there is no scale or capability trend in cross-model alignment.
All of it; there is no vision–language paired-data alignment.
All of it; there is no comparison across seeds.
A linear CKA alignment step is used as preprocessing (Sec. 3.4). Its alignment quality is not reported as a result.
All of it; there is no test of features recurring across models.
All of it; there is no test of how sensitive convergence measures are to the metric or the data.

record.verdict_notes: This is an XAI method paper. Its only contact with the claim is citing the PRH and Li et al. as representational-similarity work. The reader treated the paper's ablation of its own method and evaluation metric as a test of V6. However, BSR scores whether explanation grids find pairs closer in A than in B; it does not measure convergence between representations. All rows are therefore re-linked to none.

versions.untested_parts: Scale and capability trends across models, architectures, objectives, data, and modalities.
Alignment of image and caption representations as vision and language models improve.
Shared features or subspaces across independently initialized seeds of the same architecture.
Whether representations can be mapped or stitched with little loss, including by linear maps or without paired data.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
The study tests sensitivity to distance choices in its BSR analysis, but does not test out-of-distribution inputs or a broad range of similarity measures.
Whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete, and whether shared data or objectives explain it.
